title: The bag that copies
pages: Start with one red and one blue counter. At each step choose uniformly among the counters now present, return the chosen counter, and add one new counter of its color. After n draws the bag has n+2 counters. If r of the draws were red, its composition is (r+1) red and (n-r+1) blue. Every r from 0 through n is possible, and neither color can disappear.

This is the one-copy Pólya urn. At every fixed length n, the number of red draws is uniform on 0,1,...,n: each total has probability 1/(n+1). This does not say that color words are equally likely. A particular length-n word with r reds has probability r!(n-r)!/(n+1)!, independent of their order. There are n!/[r!(n-r)!] such words, giving the stated uniform total.

Counter identities make a finite proof visible. At successive draws there are 2, 3, ..., n+1 identities available. A history specifies the particular counter drawn each time, with new copies labeled by their birth step. All (n+1)! such histories are equally likely, although the available identities depend on the earlier draws. For n=2 there are six histories, with two histories each for zero, one, or two red draws. For n=3 there are 24 histories, six per total.

A color word such as RR merges two two-draw identity histories; RB has only one. Thus the four words RR, RB, BR, BB have probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/6, 1/3. If instead the original RB bag is restored after every draw and no copy is added, those four color words each have probability 1/4, and the red-draw totals have probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4.

The copying draws are dependent: after red, the next red chance is 2/3; after blue, it is 1/3. Yet reordering a word without changing its color totals does not change its probability. This exchangeability follows from multiplying the same red factors 1 through r and blue factors 1 through n-r over the same denominators 2 through n+1. Do not confuse it with independence.

All probability claims assume uniform selection of current identities at each step and the stated initial bag and addition rule. Deliberately choosing a legal word proves possibility, not its probability. Trial frequencies can inspire the equal-total conjecture but do not prove it. No claim about eventual loss of a color follows; both original counters remain at every finite time.

K-1: changes of composition, multiple stories with the same finish, and working backward one draw. Grades 2-3: color stories versus equally likely marked histories, and the contrast with return-only sampling. Grades 4-5: exact total distributions, equal-count reordering, and a general conjecture supported by a finite counting proof.

For ten children, prepare five opaque bags/cups and, per pair, five red plus five blue counters of equal size and feel. Only one of each begins inside. Keep the supply outside. Use removable identity labels: original counters R1 and B1; the first new copy is R2 or B2; the next is R3 or B3. The digit records when the copy was added, not the number of that color. A marker and small paper slips suffice.

Print four pages per band and supply pencils plus a small tray for each ending bag. K-1 requires counting to six, color matching, and an adult reading the questions. Middle work requires tracking two draws and distinguishing identities. Upper work uses branching counts and small products; factorial notation is optional. Have an adult enact the first copied draw and supervise resetting to exactly R1/B1 before every fresh story. Prepared, unpiloted material.

Let the group inspect RB. Deliberately take R out, visibly put that same R back, and add a second red: RB → draw R → RRB. Do a second draw so children see that both red identities can be selected. Ask, “What bags could be here after two draws?” Announce when children are choosing a possible story and when a cup is being used for a random draw.

0-7 minutes: handle counters and demonstrate returning plus copying. 7-22: choose short stories and compare final bags. 22-34: K-1 extends or reverses stories; older groups construct the six marked two-draw histories. 34-37: movement break: one child is the original counter, another joins as its copy. 37-50: compare return-only sampling or investigate three/four draws. 50-58: share an exact count or an invariant. 58-60: restore the starting kits.

A complete six-history argument is a strong endpoint. Do not insist that K-1 compute probabilities or that the oldest children enumerate 120 rows. Let the upper group use the 24-history result to predict the next stage. An unexplained five-draw guess should be recorded as a conjecture until justified.

For final bags: “How many reds were added?” For the marked tree: “After the first draw, point to each counter that could be chosen next.” For reordered words: “Which multipliers change, and which only move?” For backward work: “Which one counter could have been the last new copy?”

Janko Gravner, UC Davis MAT 235B, Martingale convergence theorems, February 2, 2024, slides 12-14, “Pólya’s urn”; university lecture PDF. The source gives the urn and uniform count law. Marked-counter histories, short-story tasks, and the exact finite keys here are independently derived classroom adaptations; no martingale theorem is a child prerequisite.

After two draws the possible bags are 3R/1B from RR, 2R/2B from RB or BR, and 1R/3B from BB. Only the middle bag has two different two-draw color stories. This is a possibility question; counting these four words as equally likely would be wrong for random copying.

For the printed choices: 4R/1B is possible via RRR; 2R/3B via RBB, BRB, or BBR; 5R/0B is impossible; 1R/4B via BBB. The full collection of possible three-draw bags also includes 3R/2B, via RRB, RBR, or BRR. The all-red picture is impossible because the original blue is never removed.

The displayed 3R/3B finish requires exactly two red draws and two blue draws. All six color stories are RRBB, RBRB, RBBR, BRRB, BRBR, BBRR. Completeness can be seen by choosing the two red positions among four: (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4).

The four-draw bags with more blue than red are exactly 1R/5B, made by BBBB, and 2R/4B, made by RBBB, BRBB, BBRB, or BBBR. The bag has six counters, with at least one of each color; the other mixtures are tied or red-majority. Children need a story for each blue-majority bag, not necessarily all four stories for the second bag.

Each last draw adds exactly one counter of its own color, so remove one candidate last copy to find a predecessor. A predecessor must still contain at least one red and one blue. For example, removing the only blue from 5R/1B would make 5R/0B, which cannot have arisen from the required start.

Copying cannot lose all blue counters, or all red counters. Every drawn counter is returned, and each move only adds a counter. In particular, the original blue remains. This is a deterministic invariant, not an observation about which color seems to be winning.
RR → 3R/1B; RB → 2R/2B; BR → 2R/2B; BB → 1R/3B. The balanced finish has two color stories; each extreme has one. Color-story counts alone do not measure probability here.

All six marked histories are listed below. Each first choice has chance 1/2; each second choice, conditional on the first, has chance 1/3. Thus every row has chance 1/6. “R2” or “B2” exists only in the corresponding first-draw branch.
All three compositions have two histories, so none has the most: each has probability 1/3. Notice that RR and BB each merge two marked histories, while RB and BR each merge one.

Copying: zero, one, two red draws are tied at 2/6 = 1/3 each. Return only: RR, RB, BR, BB are now four equally likely histories, so the totals have weights 1, 2, 1 and probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4. One red draw is most likely in the unchanged bag. Copying increases the chance of repeating the first color.

The stories are RRB, RBR, BRR. Each has chance 1/12: RRB gives (1/2)(2/3)(1/4); RBR gives (1/2)(1/3)(2/4); BRR gives (1/2)(1/3)(2/4). Each represents two of the 24 marked histories. The intermediate bags differ, but these three ordered stories have equal probabilities.

5R/1B: only RRRR, because all four added counters must be red. 4R/2B: RRBR and RBRR work; the full set is RRRB, RRBR, RBRR, BRRR. 3R/3B: RRBB and RBRB work; all six are RRBB, RBRB, RBBR, BRRB, BRBR, BBRR.
No. Draws are returned and moves only add counters. Each original color remains present after every number of draws, even when the bag becomes very unbalanced.

The six marked histories are (R1,R1), (R1,R2), (R1,B1), (B1,R1), (B1,B1), (B1,B2). Each has probability 1/6. The first two have two red draws, the middle two have one, and the last two have zero. All totals are tied, two histories each.

Without copies, the four histories are RR, RB, BR, BB, each with probability 1/4. The probabilities for zero, one, two reds become 1/4, 1/2, 1/4, compared with 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 under copying. In copying, the first color gains an extra identity for the second draw, giving RR and BB two marked histories each.

RRB, RBR, BRR each has probability 1/12. Their products are (1/2)(2/3)(1/4), (1/2)(1/3)(2/4), and (1/2)(1/3)(2/4). Reordering does not change the product of the red factors and blue factors. The draws remain dependent despite this equality.

There are six marked histories for each total 0, 1, 2, 3. BBB and RRR each have 1 × 2 × 3 = 6 identity histories. For one red, the three words RBB, BRB, BBR have two histories each, hence six. The three words with two reds also have two each. These four groups cover all eight possible color words and all 24 marked histories.

Each of the five totals has 24 of the 120 marked histories, hence chance 1/5. Extend the six histories in each three-draw group by the five available fourth-draw identities. The contributions to totals 0 through 4 are:

Predict 1/6 for each red total after five draws, and 1/(n+1) after n draws. Proof: a word with r reds has probability r!(n-r)!/(n+1)!, since its red numerators are 1,...,r and its blue numerators 1,...,n-r. There are n!/[r!(n-r)!] such words. Multiplication gives 1/(n+1). A child’s observed pattern remains a conjecture until justified; the general proof is an optional endpoint invited by the problem.
